name: Simon Sudbury
role: Archbishop of Canterbury; Lord Chancellor of England
description: Archbishop of Canterbury from 1375 and Lord Chancellor of England from 1380, in which office he bore direct administrative responsibility for the unpopular fiscal policy of the minority government, including the 1381 poll tax. It was Sudbury who had earlier imprisoned and excommunicated John Ball for heresy. When the Kentish rebels reached Canterbury on 10 June 1381 they compelled the cathedral monks to swear loyalty to the commons in his absence; he had already withdrawn to the Tower of London with the King. On 14 June, while Richard II was at Mile End, a separate rebel force of roughly 400 entered the Tower without resistance, found Sudbury in the chapel of St John, dragged him to Tower Hill, and beheaded him without trial -- reportedly requiring several strokes. His head was displayed on London Bridge, his archbishop's mitre nailed to his skull.
narrative_function: The revolt's highest-ranking victim; his killing marks the point at which the rising becomes irrevocably violent against the state's senior officers.
